questions.title: Java Reflection API
questions.question: What is Java Reflection and what are its use cases and limitations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Reflection: inspect and manipulate classes, methods, fields at runtime**
- **Use cases: frameworks (Spring DI, Jackson, Hibernate), testing (Mockito), annotation processing**
- **Performance overhead: slower than direct calls — not for hot paths**
- **Breaks encapsulation: can access private fields/methods**
- **Modern alternative: `java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle` — faster than reflection**
- **Red flag:** recommending reflection for application business logic — it's a framework tool

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Reflection allows Java code to inspect and manipulate classes, methods, constructors, and fields at runtime — things that are normally determined at compile time. You can discover class structure, invoke methods by name, access private fields, and instantiate objects from class names stored as strings.

It's the foundation of most Java frameworks: Spring uses reflection to discover beans and inject dependencies, Jackson uses it to serialize/deserialize objects to JSON, Hibernate maps entity fields to database columns, and JUnit discovers and runs test methods — all without you writing explicit wiring code.

The main limitation is performance: reflection calls are significantly slower than direct method calls because the JVM can't optimize them as aggressively (no JIT inlining). They also bypass compile-time checks and encapsulation. Use reflection only in framework infrastructure code — never in hot business logic paths.

questions.title: Custom Annotations
questions.question: How do you create and process custom annotations in Java?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@interface` declaration, `@Target`, `@Retention`, `@Documented`**
- **`RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME`:** available for reflection processing
- **`RetentionPolicy.CLASS`:** in bytecode, not at runtime (APT processing)
- **`RetentionPolicy.SOURCE`:** compile-only, like `@Override`
- **Processing: reflection (runtime) vs `javax.annotation.processing.Processor` (compile-time)**
- **Spring AOP + `@Around` for annotation-based cross-cutting concerns**
- **Red flag:** using `RetentionPolicy.CLASS` when you want runtime processing — annotation won't be visible

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Custom annotations in Java are declared with `@interface`. The `@Target` meta-annotation specifies where the annotation can be placed — on methods, classes, fields. `@Retention` controls how long the annotation survives: `SOURCE` is discarded after compilation, `CLASS` is in the bytecode but not loaded into the JVM, `RUNTIME` is available through reflection.

For runtime annotation processing — the most common case — use `@Retention(RUNTIME)` and inspect with reflection. Spring's `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, and `@Async` all work this way: Spring uses AOP to intercept annotated methods at runtime.

For custom annotations that add behavior, combine with Spring AOP: declare a pointcut that matches your annotation, implement the advice in `@Around`, and Spring weaves it at bean creation time. This is how you implement audit logging, rate limiting, or access checks declaratively.

questions.title: Compile-Time Annotation Processing
questions.question: What is Java annotation processing (APT) and how do tools like Lombok use it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **APT (Annotation Processing Tool): runs during compilation — generates code from annotations**
- **`javax.annotation.processing.Processor`: implement to create custom processors**
- **Lombok uses APT: `@Getter`, `@Builder`, `@Data` generate bytecode at compile time**
- **MapStruct uses APT: generates type-safe mapper implementations**
- **`RetentionPolicy.SOURCE` or `CLASS`:** for APT (not needed at runtime)
- **Red flag:** confusing APT with runtime reflection — they're completely different mechanisms

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Annotation Processing Tool (APT) runs during the `javac` compilation phase — it reads annotations and generates new Java source files or modifies bytecode before compilation completes. This is entirely different from runtime reflection, which reads annotations after compilation.

Lombok works through APT: when you write `@Data` on a class, Lombok's annotation processor reads it during compilation and adds `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, getters, and setters directly into the compiled bytecode — before the class is even fully compiled. The generated code behaves exactly like code you wrote manually.

MapStruct similarly generates type-safe mapper implementations at compile time — instead of runtime reflection for mapping DTO to entity, it generates explicit field-by-field mapping code that's as fast as handwritten code.

The advantage of APT over runtime reflection: zero runtime overhead, full compile-time type checking, and IDE auto-completion on generated code.
